summary: End-to-end encryption and signing of email is flexible, which can trap users with surprising failures. This informational RFC gives guidance to Mail User Agent implementers on avoiding those risks, so users of cryptographically protected email are less likely to be caught out.

eli5.summary: Locking your mail has lots of options and some are tricky. This is advice for people who make email programs on how to avoid confusing and unsafe results.

questions: how should mail clients handle encrypted email
how to properly sign and encrypt email messages
what is a cryptographic envelope in email
subtitle: Best practices for implementing secure email with encryption and digital signatures.

tldr.problem: Email encryption and signing standards are flexible but can trap users with surprising failures like signature breakage, accidental leakage of encrypted content, and confusing user interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: This informational RFC provides detailed guidance to Mail User Agent implementers on how to safely compose and interpret cryptographically protected email, including rules for message structure, certificate handling, and error cases.
tldr.outcome: Systems following this guidance provide stronger security properties and better interoperability, though some challenges like certificate discovery and cross-MUA key synchronization remain unsolved.

facts.label: Affected systems
facts.value: Mail User Agents with S/MIME or PGP/MIME support

today: RFC 9787 is an Informational RFC that provides guidance to current and future MUA implementations. It remains the primary reference for best practices in end-to-end email security, though it identifies several unsolved problems including certificate discovery mechanisms, cross-MUA key synchronization, and webmail threat models.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
End-to-end email security using S/MIME and PGP/MIME can provide integrity, authentication, and confidentiality to MIME email messages. However, there are many ways that a Mail User Agent (MUA) can misinterpret or accidentally break these security guarantees. This RFC offers guidance to MUA implementers to help avoid these problems.

The document defines key terminology including Cryptographic Layer (a MIME substructure that supplies cryptographic protections), Cryptographic Envelope (the contiguous set of layers starting from the outermost MIME type), Cryptographic Payload (the first non-cryptographic layer within the envelope), and Cryptographic Summary (the overall cryptographic status of the message).

MUAs are divided into three profiles: non-cryptographic (no cryptographic capabilities), conformant (following this guidance), and legacy (has capabilities but does not adhere to this guidance).
sections.eli5: There are different ways to lock an email, and the person who writes the email program needs to know all the ways things can go wrong so they can stop it from happening.

sections.title: Usability Principles
sections.content:
Any MUA that enables users to transition from unprotected messages to cryptographically protected messages needs to consider how the user understands this transition. The primary goal of an MUA user is communication, so interface elements that interfere with communication should be avoided. Users must be able to understand which protections any given message has.

The RFC recommends keeping cryptographic protections simple by applying them to the entire message as a whole, not just to some subparts. The standard message composition interface should offer minimal controls indicating which types of protection to apply. Similarly, the rendering interface should offer a minimal, clear indicator about the end-to-end cryptographic status of the entire message.

Users expect end-to-end cryptographic protection to retain the familiar experience of email itself. An MUA should not inadvertently limit the ability of users to interact with correspondents who use legacy or non-cryptographic MUAs. The RFC also discusses how to handle the transition between showing which messages are secure versus warning about insecure messages.
sections.eli5: Keep it simple so the person using the email program understands what's locked and what's not, without too many buttons and choices.

sections.title: Cryptographic Message Structure
sections.content:
The RFC establishes conventions for understanding message structure in both S/MIME and PGP/MIME. S/MIME supports four forms of cryptographic layers: multipart/signed (authentication and integrity), PKCS #7 signed-data (authentication and integrity), enveloped-data (confidentiality), and authEnveloped-data (confidentiality and integrity).

PGP/MIME supports two forms: signing (multipart/signed with PGP signature providing authenticity and integrity) and encryption (multipart/encrypted with application/octet-stream offering confidentiality, confidentiality with integrity, or all three together).

A critical concept is the Cryptographic Envelope: the largest contiguous set of cryptographic layers starting from the outermost MIME type. If a non-cryptographic layer intervenes, any cryptographic layers within it are Errant Cryptographic Layers that must not contribute to the message's overall cryptographic state. The RFC defines a simplified mental model for users: Unprotected, Verified (valid signature), Confidential (encrypted with valid signature), and an error state for Encrypted But Unverified messages.
sections.eli5: Different ways to lock an email create different layers, and if something goes wrong with one layer, it can break the whole lock.

sections.title: Message Composition
sections.content:
When composing a cryptographically protected message, the MUA should follow specific procedures to ensure proper Cryptographic Envelope and Payload. The basic algorithm applies cryptographic protections to the message body, then adds non-structural header fields (like Subject and To). A conformant MUA must implement Header Protection as described in RFC 9788 to protect message headers as well.

When both signing and encrypting, the signature must be inside the encryption (encryption outside, signature inside). This ensures the signature details remain confidential and prevents mail transport agents from accidentally breaking the signature. A conformant MUA must not generate encrypted-only messages deliberately; it should offer only three composition choices: no protection, signed only (Verified), or signed and encrypted (Confidential).

When replying to encrypted messages, the MUA must either compose the reply encrypted or avoid including quoted text from the original message to prevent leaking the cleartext of the encrypted message. If the composing MUA cannot encrypt the reply, it should strip the quoted text unless the user explicitly indicates they are deliberately including previously confidential content in a non-confidential message.
sections.eli5: When writing a locked email, put the signature inside the lock, and don't send a copy that's locked and a copy that's not locked to different people.

sections.title: Message Interpretation and Pitfalls
sections.content:
A well-formed message has a Cryptographic Envelope, a Cryptographic Payload, and no Errant Cryptographic Layers. When rendering such a message, the MUA evaluates the cryptographic properties and displays the Cryptographic Summary in a secure, strictly controlled part of the UI that cannot be spoofed by the message content itself. The Cryptographic Payload is rendered as though it is the body of the message.

The RFC describes how to handle errant cryptographic layers. If a message contains an errant signing layer, replace it with the protected part when rendering. For errant encryption layers, the MUA should decrypt but not indicate in the Cryptographic Summary that the message was encrypted, and must not merge the decrypted data with other parts. Special handling applies to mailing list footers appended to signed messages: the MUA may indicate the message is verified but must clearly distinguish the footer from the protected part.

The RFC also discusses signature failures (the message is treated as unprotected), weak encryption (the user must be warned), and forwarded messages with their own cryptographic protection (which must not be conflated with the outer message's protection).
sections.eli5: When reading a locked email, make sure the lock is real and not broken, and don't let fake locks fool the person reading it.

sections.title: Certificate Management
sections.content:
A cryptographically capable MUA must maintain knowledge about certificates for the user's own accounts and for peers. When selecting a peer certificate for encryption, the MUA must verify that the certificate is valid (not expired or revoked), has the correct email address in its subjectAltName, has a known encryption algorithm, and includes appropriate key usage extensions.

For local certificates, S/MIME users should have separate signing and encryption certificates to avoid cross-protocol key misuse. An MUA may import PKCS #12 objects and should warn users if a bundle uses the same key for both encryption and signing. PGP/MIME users can use a single self-signed certificate with distinct subkeys for signing and encryption.

The RFC recommends that MUAs help users generate, acquire, or import certificates with minimum difficulty, and should include copies of the user's certificates in outbound messages to facilitate future communication. For S/MIME, this means including signing certificates, encryption certificates, peer certificates for reply-all functionality, and intermediate CA certificates in the signed message. The MUA should also warn users or proactively fix issues when certificates are about to expire.
sections.eli5: The program needs to know which keys belong to which person and keep track of when they expire, so locked emails can be sent to the right person.
